citations.narrative:
The facility’s acquisition and disposition records involving sugar gliders have not been accurately recorded, with various
inconsistencies identified. During this inspection, the facility showed APHIS officials acquisition records for a total of
fourteen sugar gliders on October 25, 2025, but previous records documented by the facility stated ten sugar gliders were
permanently acquired on this date. The facility originally stated the line-item count of twelve was an error and should have
recorded ten sugar gliders instead. Upon following-up the next day to confirm correct counts, the facility stated the total
count of fourteen was correct, and they’d received twelve sugar gliders, with two births occurring while in their possession.
When asked where the acquisition records were for the two births, the facility stated they did not have them.
The remaining two sugar glider records documented dates of disposition that conflicted with the information previously
provided by the facility. The facility previously stated all of the sugar gliders were dispositioned prior to December 11,
2025. However, these two disposition records reported dates of December 13, 2025 and March 1, 2026. When reviewing
the disposition record dates for these last two records, the facility stated the dates were recorded incorrectly.
Acquisition and disposition records, including offspring born at the facility, are necessary to accurately track and identify
animals being used in regulated activities, as well as aid in the detection of movement of animals upon relocation to a new
site. The licensee shall make, keep, and maintain records of acquisition/disposition of all animals that fully and correctly
disclose the required information, as outlined in this section.
Correct by October 19, 2026.

Two outdoor enclosures housing one aardwolf and three red kangaroos were not enclosed by a perimeter fence nor
included in the facility’s current perimeter fence variance:
- The screened-in enclosed porch structure housing one aardwolf serves as its primary enclosure and is attached to the
main residence.
- Three red kangaroos were moved to an enclosure that is not encompassed by a perimeter fence. While the facility has
submitted a perimeter fence variance request to the Administrator, this request has not been reviewed or approved at the
time of this inspection.
Having a perimeter fence in place protects the animals in the facility by restricting animals and unauthorized persons from
going through it or under it, permitting contact with the animals in the facility by unauthorized animals or patrons visiting
the facility. Additionally, it serves as a secondary containment system for the animals in the facility. The perimeter fence
must be sufficient distance from the outside of the primary enclosure to prevent physical contact between animals inside
the enclosure and animals or persons outside the perimeter fence. Non-dangerous animals being housed outdoors
require a 6-foot-tall perimeter fence around their enclosure and must be at least 3-feet away from the primary enclosure,
unless an approved variance has been issued in writing by the Administrator.
Correct by November 20, 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the licensees.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:

APHIS Animal Care (AC)
U.S. Department of Agriculture
2150 Centre Avenue, Building B
Mailstop #3W11
Fort Collins, CO 80526-8117
Additional Inspectors:
Rebecca Nanney, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
